The Monroe Doctrine. President James Monroe's declaration in 1823 that the Western Hemisphere was closed to further European colonization and that any attempt by European powers to interfere in the Americas would be regarded as a threat to United States security. Though the United States lacked the military power to enforce it at the time, the doctrine became foundational to American foreign policy and hemispheric supremacy, undergirding a century of United States intervention in Latin America.

Monroe announced the doctrine in December 1823 in his annual message to Congress. It was drafted primarily by Secretary of State John Quincy Adams, who shaped much of its language and strategic thinking. The doctrine declared that European powers could not establish new colonies in the Western Hemisphere and that the United States would interpret such attempts as hostile acts against American sovereignty. Monroe also asserted that the United States would not interfere in European colonial possessions or the internal affairs of existing European nations, staking a position of non-interference in Europe.

The doctrine responded to specific threats of the moment: Russian expansion claims in the Pacific Northwest, the threat of European intervention in Spanish America, and the wave of Latin American independence movements that created power vacuums in the Western Hemisphere. Initially the doctrine had little enforcement power. The United States Navy was not yet strong enough to back up such bold claims. However, the doctrine gained credibility as United States naval and economic strength grew throughout the nineteenth century. By the late 1800s, the Monroe Doctrine had become the foundation for American claims to hemispheric hegemony and shaped United States relations with Latin America for generations, establishing the United States as the dominant regional power.

Later presidents invoked and reinterpreted the doctrine. Most notably, Theodore Roosevelt added the Roosevelt Corollary, asserting the United States right to intervene in Latin American affairs to maintain order and prevent European intervention. The Monroe Doctrine remains an iconic statement of United States foreign policy, cited throughout history to justify both intervention and non-intervention alike, shaping American diplomatic tradition and serving as a powerful statement of American intentions in the Western Hemisphere.
